# The agents layer

This directory adds to the x86-64 [GNU system](../Readme.md) the programs a person uses to work with a coding agent over SSH: each vendor's published build, fetched for the person who builds the image, checked against the digest its vendor publishes, and installed unmodified under its own license. Nothing of a package is committed but its recipe. The layer has five packages, GitHub's `gh`, Anthropic's Claude Code, `claude`, Meta's Muse Code, `muse`, OpenAI's Codex, `codex`, and Google's Antigravity CLI, `agy`. A package is installed only when the builder names it.

## Use

`GNU_AGENTS` lists the packages the GNU root gets, by the names of their recipes in [`packages/`](packages), or is `all` for every package; it is empty by default. The packages are x86-64 programs, so the variable needs `ARCH=x86_64`:

    make ARCH=x86_64 GNU_AGENTS=gh os-real-gnu-ext2
    make ARCH=x86_64 GNU_AGENTS=all machine

`make ARCH=x86_64 GNU_AGENTS=gh gnu-agents` fetches and stages the packages without building the root. A change to the list, to a recipe or to `fetch_agents.sh` builds the root again; [`mk/gnu-agents.mk`](../../../mk/gnu-agents.mk) has the rules. The release to the installed machine builds with `GNU_AGENTS=all` (`tools/flow/release.sh`), and so does the root `tests/run agents` boots, `os-real-gnu-agents.ext2`.

On the machine each package is a directory of `/opt`, as its vendor published it, with a link to its program in `/usr/bin` and `/bin`. Its page in the manual says how to sign in over SSH and where the credentials are kept: [gh(1)](../../../man/man1/gh.1), [claude(1)](../../../man/man1/claude.1), [codex(1)](../../../man/man1/codex.1), [muse(1)](../../../man/man1/muse.1) and [agy(1)](../../../man/man1/agy.1).

After a release has installed the layer on the Lenovo, the owner signs in to each program there over SSH, as an ordinary account and as its page says: `claude auth login`, `codex login --device-auth`, `muse login`, `gh auth login`, and for Antigravity CLI its first session, `agy`, which offers Google OAuth. The acceptance then runs from the owner's computer, in a clone of this tree:

    sh tests/system/accept/agents_accept.sh lenovo USER

USER is the account signed in to, reached by ssh's own key or the one `RACH2_ACCEPT_KEY` names; the machine is at 192.168.0.106 unless a third argument or `RACH2_MACHINE_ADDRESS` names another address, and `RACH2_ACCEPT_AGENTS` may name fewer agents than `claude codex agy muse`. For each agent the script makes a disposable repository, `~/rach2-accept/AGENT`, and in the agent's screen, in tmux over SSH, asks it to read the repository's notes, change a file, run the repository's test and commit, then cancels a turn, resizes the terminal, drops and makes again the SSH connection, and reopens the conversation. Then it reboots the Lenovo and requires each selected program's sign-in, version and file, and gh's, to be as they were, and each selected agent to answer one request. Only those programs' credential files are required and scanned for strings in the log. The script prints a line for each step and ends with `agents-accept: PASS` or `agents-accept: FAIL (N)`; its log, `build/images/agents-accept-lenovo.log`, has the screens and answers it read, each passed first through a filter on the machine that replaces every string of a credential file, and the script checks there that the log has none of them. [`agents_accept.sh`](../../../tests/system/accept/agents_accept.sh) describes each step in its header.

A package keeps its vendor's license, which the recipe names in `LICENSE` and installs beside the program; `NOTICES` lists those files, and the stage fails without them. Meta publishes no license file for Muse Code, so its recipe writes `/opt/muse/TERMS`, which names the terms and gives their address. Google publishes no license file with `agy` either, so its recipe writes `/opt/agy/TERMS`, which names the three documents that govern its use: the Google Terms of Service, the [Google Antigravity Additional Terms of Service](https://antigravity.google/terms) and the Google Privacy Policy. Claude Code is proprietary: the recipe fetches it for the person who builds the image, and nothing of it is redistributed. Codex's package has the licenses of its voice libraries but not OpenAI's own or those of its other helpers, so its recipe fetches OpenAI's license and notice and bubblewrap's license from the Codex sources at the release's tag, ripgrep's from its tag 15.2.0 and zsh's from the commit the release builds, each pinned by its SHA-256. The recipes and `fetch_agents.sh` are in-house.

## Design

### Recipes

A recipe, `packages/NAME.sh`, is a shell fragment that [`fetch_agents.sh`](fetch_agents.sh) reads in a shell of its own. Its header comment says what the program is, where it comes from and how it is pinned. It sets:

* `VERSION`, the version the vendor published.
* `LICENSE`, the license's short name.
* `FILES`, one line for each download: the name it is kept under, its URL, and its digest as the vendor publishes it, `sha256:HEX` or `sha512:HEX`.
* `NOTICES`, the license and notice files, as paths in the stage.

It defines `package_stage DIR`, which lays the package out under `DIR` as the root has it, taking each download through `fetched NAME`. It may define `package_verify`, which checks the vendor's signature on a download, and `package_check DIR`, which runs the staged program on the build host. Both may write in `SCRATCH`, an empty directory of the package's own, which the program may take as its home.

### Fetching and staging

`fetch_agents.sh NAME...` downloads each file of `FILES` once into `../downloads/agents/NAME/`, which Git ignores, and checks it against its digest each time `fetched` names it, so a download is checked again at every use; a file with another digest is removed and refused. It then makes `SCRATCH`, runs `package_verify`, stages the package from nothing into `agents/NAME/` of the layer's build tree, `build/x86_64/vendor/gnu/agents/NAME/`, checks that each of `NOTICES` is there, runs `package_check`, and removes `SCRATCH`. Make runs it behind a stamp for each package, `agents/NAME.stamp`.

### Installing

[`install_root.sh`](../install_root.sh) copies each stage that `GNU_AGENTS` names into the root after the Chromium packages, and refuses a file the root already has, as it does for every part of the layer. Its later steps give each program of `/usr/bin` its name in `/bin`.

### gh

`gh` is a static Go executable and needs no library of the root. Under `/opt/gh` it has `bin/gh`, its manual pages in `share/man/man1` and `LICENSE`. Measured on Linux, it starts no other process for `--version`, `auth status` or `api`. It writes its settings to `~/.config/gh`, and a device identifier and the state of its update check to `~/.local/state/gh`. Before a request it asks the Secret Service of the D-Bus session bus for a stored token, at the address `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` gives or at `/run/user/UID/bus`, and reads the token from `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml` where there is none. It talks to `api.github.com` and `github.com`, or to the host `GH_HOST` names, whose API it reaches at `https://HOST/api/v3/`, and trusts the certificate authorities of `/etc/ssl/certs`, with those of the file `SSL_CERT_FILE` names. It does not update itself: on a terminal it checks GitHub for a newer release once a day and prints a notice, which `GH_NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER` turns off. Its telemetry, on by default, is turned off by `gh config set telemetry disabled` or `GH_TELEMETRY=false`.

### claude

Claude Code is one executable of 257 MB, a program for Bun, a JavaScript runtime, with the runtime and its scripts in the file. Under `/opt/claude` it has `bin/claude` and `LICENSE.md`, and the recipe adds the managed settings, `/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json`, which come before every other setting. Anthropic's setup page describes the signed manifest that `package_verify` checks: the key is published armored, `gpgv` reads it as a binary keyring, which is the armor's base64 body, and the fingerprint of the key that made the signature is the last field of `gpgv`'s `VALIDSIG` status line. The binary must then have the SHA-256 that the manifest lists under `platforms.linux-x64.checksum`.

What follows was measured with 2.1.296 on the testing host, Ubuntu under WSL 2, under `strace` and behind a proxy that logged each request, in a fresh home. Under WSL every command also runs Windows' `reg.exe` to read Anthropic's policy keys in the registry, which it does not do where there is no WSL.

* Libraries: it links against glibc 2.26 or later, `libc.so.6`, `libm.so.6`, `libpthread.so.0`, `libdl.so.2`, `librt.so.1` and `ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, which the GNU root has. It reads the certificate authorities of `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` and `/etc/ssl/certs`, with those of the file `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` names.
* Processes: `--version`, `--help` and `auth status` start none, nor does `update` with the managed settings. A session runs `/bin/bash -c -l` once to save the login shell's environment, and each command of its Bash tool as `/bin/bash -c` with that saved environment; it runs `git` on the repository, its own file under the name `rg` for ripgrep, which it has built in, `uname`, and `gh auth token` and a `gh issue list` of the user's closed issues on `anthropics/claude-code` when the path finds `gh`. `claude doctor`, and `claude update` without the managed settings, run `npm -g config get prefix` where the path finds `npm`.
* Files: `--version` and `--help` write nothing. The other commands, `auth status` among them, write `~/.claude.json`, its settings and the state of each project, through a temporary file and a rename under the lock `~/.claude.json.lock`, and `~/.claude/`: `sessions/`, `backups/`, `cache/`, `projects/` with the transcripts, `plugins/` with Anthropic's catalog of plugins, and `.credentials.json`, mode 0600, after a sign-in. `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` names another directory for `~/.claude`. A session also makes `claude-UID/` and `cc-socks/`, with a socket for each session, under `TMPDIR`, or `/tmp`.
* Hosts: the model's requests go to `api.anthropic.com`, or to `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. A session with no sign-in and the settings as the vendor ships them also reached `api.anthropic.com` for its start-up settings, the list of MCP servers, feature flags and usage events; `http-intake.logs.us5.datadoghq.com` for its logs; `downloads.claude.ai` for its update, `/claude-code-releases/latest` and then the new version's `manifest.json` and binary, and for the catalog of plugins; `raw.githubusercontent.com` for the change log of `anthropics/claude-code`; and, at the first start, `platform.claude.com`. `claude auth login` gives an address at `claude.com/cai/oauth/authorize` to open in a browser. It takes a proxy from `HTTPS_PROXY`.
* Updates: as shipped, a session fetches `latest` from `downloads.claude.ai` at its start and installs a newer version into `~/.local/share/claude/versions/` for the next start, and `claude update` and `claude install` do the same on demand. With `DISABLE_UPDATES` set to 1 in the managed settings, as the recipe writes them, a session fetched no release, and `claude update` and `claude install` printed `Updates are disabled by your administrator` and exited with status 0 without fetching a release, at once with no network as well; `claude doctor` reports `Auto-updates: disabled (set by env: DISABLE_UPDATES)`. `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` alone stops only the background update.
* Telemetry: usage events go to `api.anthropic.com/api/event_logging/`, logs to Datadog, and feature flags come from `api.anthropic.com/api/eval/`; `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` stopped all three. `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1` stopped every request of the session but the download of the catalog of plugins, which `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_OFFICIAL_MARKETPLACE_AUTOINSTALL=1` stopped too. The recipe sets neither; [claude(1)](../../../man/man1/claude.1) gives the settings to the person who uses it.
* Sandbox: the managed settings set `sandbox.enabled` to false, Claude Code's default, since its sandbox needs bubblewrap, which the GNU root does not have.

### muse

Muse Code is one static executable of 376 MB, which needs no library of the root. Meta's installer, `https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh`, puts a launcher script at `~/.local/bin/muse`. The launcher reads the channel manifest, `https://api.meta.ai/muse-code/channels/muse-stable`, for the current version and its release manifest, downloads the file that manifest lists for the platform, checks its size and SHA-256, keeps it beside itself as `muse-bin-VERSION` and runs it. Each time it starts it looks for a newer launcher and a newer version, at most once an hour, and installs them in the background; `MUSE_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1` turns that off. The program has no update code of its own, so the layer installs it without the launcher, and it stays at the version the recipe pins.

Measured on Linux, `--version` and `--help` start no other process and write no file. Its screen asks whether to trust the directory it starts in, and writes the answer to `~/.config/muse/trust.json`. It makes `~/.local/share/muse`, with a SQLite index of its sessions, the sessions, its bundled skills and plugins and a log of each start, and makes and removes scratch directories under `TMPDIR` or `/tmp`. To learn whether its sandbox works it runs `/usr/bin/bwrap`, where there is one, and itself as `muse __tbh_internal_bwrap`, its own copy of bubblewrap; it also reads `/etc/ssh/ssh_config`. With no credential it offers two sign-ins: by browser, a device code that `auth.meta.com` confirms, for which it runs `xdg-open` on the address and also prints it, or by a Model API key typed in. A key in `META_API_KEY` signs it in without either and takes priority over a stored credential, which it keeps in `~/.config/muse/auth.json`. Its settings are `~/.config/muse/settings.json`, where `"telemetry": {"enabled": false}` turns off its telemetry. It talks to `api.meta.ai` and `auth.meta.com`, or to the server `--base-url` names, and trusts as well the certificate authority whose file the setting `endpoint_transport.ca_bundle` names.

### codex

Codex is a static Rust executable built for musl. Under `/opt/codex` it has the files of OpenAI's package as the release has them: `bin/codex`, `bin/codex-code-mode-host`, `codex-path/rg`, `codex-resources/bwrap`, `codex-resources/zsh/bin/zsh`, the voice host with its libraries in `codex-resources/voice`, and `codex-package.json`, which names the program and the two directories. Codex finds its helpers from the path of its own program, which it reads from `/proc/self/exe`, so `/usr/bin/codex` is a link to `/opt/codex/bin/codex`. Its zsh and its voice host link against glibc, which the root has. Beside the package are `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` and `licenses/`, with the licenses of ripgrep, bubblewrap and zsh.

Codex reads its settings from its system configuration file, `/etc/codex/config.toml`, which the recipe writes, then from `~/.codex/config.toml` and the command line, each over the one before. It writes its state to `~/.codex`, or to the directory `CODEX_HOME` names: its settings, an installation identifier, SQLite databases of its sessions and logs, the credentials of a sign-in in `auth.json`, and in `tmp/arg0` links to its own program under the names of the commands it runs as, such as `apply_patch`, which it does not make in a home under `/tmp`. It talks to `api.openai.com` with an API key, and to `chatgpt.com` and `auth.openai.com` with a ChatGPT sign-in. With an API key too, a session fetches the catalog of plugins as it starts and again as it ends: `/backend-api/plugins/featured` and `/backend-api/plugins/export/curated` from `chatgpt.com`, and `/repos/openai/plugins` from `api.github.com`; the feature `plugins`, which `codex features disable plugins` turns off, makes all three. As it starts, its screen also fetches a notice to show, `/openai/codex/main/announcement_tip.toml` from `raw.githubusercontent.com`, which `tui.show_tooltips = false` does not stop. Codex trusts the system's certificate authorities, with those of the file `CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE` names, or `SSL_CERT_FILE` where it is unset.

Measured on Linux, offline, with Codex's screen showing its sign-in menu in tmux, Codex 0.162.1 with no settings is three processes. The screen, `/opt/codex/bin/codex`, has 110 MB resident. Before it draws, it copies the whole package, 430 MB, to `~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/0.162.1-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` and starts two processes from the copy: the shared server, `codex app-server --listen unix:// --analytics-default-enabled --managed-daemon`, 245 MB, which runs the sessions for every screen of the user and for `codex agents`; and its updater, `codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop`, 190 MB, which from five minutes after it starts runs `https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh` to install a newer release beside the copy and restarts the server from it. Both outlive the screen. The recipe's settings make it one process of 120 MB and no copy:

* `features.daemon_auto_start = false`, a feature that `codex features list` shows and `codex features disable` sets, starts no server, so the screen runs its sessions in its own process. The documented option `--no-daemon` does the same for one run, and so does a `-c` option on the command line other than a few feature switches. `check_for_update_on_startup = false` alone leaves all three processes.
* `check_for_update_on_startup = false` keeps the screen from asking `api.github.com` for the latest release when it starts, and from offering an update. Codex counts `/opt/codex` as a local build, which it does not update in any case.
* `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` runs the commands the model asks for without Codex's sandbox. On Linux the sandbox is the bundled bubblewrap, which Codex runs through `/proc/self/fd/N`, and which needs capability bounding sets, `/proc/sys/kernel/overflowuid` and `pivot_root`, which Rach2 does not have.

### agy

`agy` is Google's build of Antigravity CLI, a dynamically linked x86-64 executable for glibc of 220,553,472 bytes, written in Go with BoringCrypto. It needs `libc.so.6`, `libpthread.so.0`, `libdl.so.2`, `libm.so.6`, `librt.so.1` and `libresolv.so.2`, which the root has. Under `/opt/agy` it has `bin/agy`, the one file of Google's tarball, `antigravity`, under the name Google's installer gives it, and `TERMS`. The installer also runs `agy install`, which adds the program's directory to the shell's startup files; the recipe does not, since `/usr/bin` has the link.

Measured on Linux, it starts no other process for `--version`, `--help` or its screen up to the sign-in, and a session run with `-p` leaves none behind. `--version` and `--help` write nothing. Its first session writes about 17 MB to `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/`, with its settings, conversations, logs, cache and an installation identifier, and to `~/.gemini/config/`, with its projects. Among them are helpers it unpacks from itself into `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/bin/`: `webm_encoder`, an executable whose interpreter is `/usr/grte/v5/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, a path that Debian, Ubuntu and this root lack, and, after a session that runs a command, `agentapi`, a shell script. It trusts the certificate authorities of `/etc/ssl/certs`, or in their place those of the file `SSL_CERT_FILE` names, as Go's runtime does.

A session that is not signed in offers two ways to sign in: Google OAuth, for a Google account, and a Google Cloud project. With Google OAuth it prints the address of Google's sign-in page and waits for the code the page shows once the person has signed in, so a machine without a browser signs in from any other computer. It keeps the token in the Secret Service of the D-Bus session bus where one answers, and otherwise in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/antigravity-oauth-token`. With `"modelProvider": "gemini"` in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json` and a key in `GEMINI_API_KEY` it needs no sign-in and sends its requests to the Gemini API, or to the server that `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` names.

Its updater runs in the background and replaces the program with Google's newest release. It first creates a file in the program's directory, and stops when it cannot, as an ordinary user cannot write `/opt/agy/bin`. `AGY_CLI_DISABLE_AUTO_UPDATE=true`, the setting Google documents, turns it off: the stage's `/etc/profile.d/agy.sh` sets it, and the root's `/etc/profile` reads that directory, so every login shell has it. A command that `ssh` runs without a login shell does not.

Each session sends Google usage events and asks a server for feature flags. Measured on Linux, a session of `-p` posts about 62 kB in two requests to `https://play.googleapis.com/log`, and registers with `antigravity-unleash.goog`, a server of the Unleash feature-flag protocol, and fetches the flags from it. Google documents `"enableTelemetry": false` in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json` as the setting that turns metrics off, but version 1.4.0 writes the file again without that member at each start, headless or in its screen, and sends the same events whether it is false, true or absent. Google documents no other setting that stops either. With neither server reachable, or with each answering 404, the program works on as before.

## Building

The layer builds where the rest of the GNU layer does, on an x86-64 Linux host, with access to each vendor's download site. Besides the tools the [GNU layer](../Readme.md#building) lists it needs `sha512sum`, or `shasum`, for a package pinned by SHA-512, and `gpgv` and `base64` for Claude Code's signature. The check of Codex's signature also needs access to Sigstore's repository of its trusted root, `tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev`, from which `cosign` fetches the root into a scratch home. Codex's downloads are 300 MB, its stage 440 MB.

## Updating

To update a package, take the new version's digest from the list its vendor publishes, verifying the list's signature where the vendor signs it, and set `VERSION` and the digest in the recipe. For Claude Code, fetch the new release's `manifest.json` and `manifest.json.sig`, verify the signature by [Anthropic's procedure](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup#verify-the-manifest-signature) with the key whose fingerprint is `FINGERPRINT`, and set the binary's digest from the manifest's `linux-x64` entry, the digests of the manifest and its signature, and the npm package's `dist.integrity` from `https://registry.npmjs.org/@anthropic-ai/claude-code/VERSION`, decoded from base64 to hex. A new key changes `FINGERPRINT` only after its fingerprint is checked against the setup page. For Codex these are the line of `codex-package_SHA256SUMS` for the package and the digests the release's API lists for the package's `.sigstore` bundle; the bundle's certificate must name the release workflow of the new tag, which `package_verify` requires. The license files come again from the new tag, and from the ripgrep version and the zsh commit that the tag's `scripts/codex_package/rg` and `.github/workflows/rust-release-zsh.yml` name. Then update the package's row in the table above, its page in the manual and what its row in `tests/system/agents/` expects, and run `ARCH=x86_64 tests/run agents`.

A new package is a recipe in `packages/`, a row in `tests/system/agents/`, with a script for the fake server where the row talks to the vendor's service, a page in [`man/`](../../../man/Readme.md), a line in the table above and a section of Design that records what the program needs.

## Limits

* The packages are x86-64 programs, and the layer installs them only in the x86-64 GNU root.
* Claude Code's sandbox is off, and its shell commands run with the user's own rights, until the GNU root has bubblewrap and the kernel what bubblewrap needs.
* GitHub signs no file of `gh`'s release. Its build provenance attestations are checked by `gh attestation verify`, which needs a sign-in, so the recipe pins the digest the checksums file lists.
* Meta signs neither manifest of Muse Code's release, so the recipe pins the digest the release manifest lists. Meta's terms let the person who fetched the program install and use it, and forbid giving it to anyone else: a root built with `muse` is not to be given away.
* Muse Code's sandbox, its own copy of bubblewrap, needs parts of Linux that Rach2 does not have yet, among them `pivot_root` and `/proc/sys/kernel/overflowuid`; on Rach2 it is turned off with `--disable-sandbox` or `--yolo`.
* Codex runs the model's commands with no sandbox, as the user who runs it, until Rach2 has what bubblewrap needs.

## Tests

`fetch_agents.sh` runs each recipe's `package_check` on the build host when it stages the package. `ARCH=x86_64 tests/run agents` boots `os-real-gnu-agents.ext2` with 4 GiB of memory on a network whose only route out is to the fake API server on the host ([`tests/system/fakeapi/fakeapi.py`](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/fakeapi.py)), and runs the rows of [`tests/system/agents/`](../../../tests/system/agents) over SSH as the test account; [`tests/system/suites/agents.sh`](../../../tests/system/suites/agents.sh) describes a row and its script for the server. The `gh` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and its license, `gh auth status` with no account signed in, one HTTPS request from `gh api` with no account to openssl's test server on the machine, which `gh` refuses until `SSL_CERT_FILE` names the server's certificate, and `GH_TOKEN=invalid gh api user` against the fake server as `api.github.com`, which answers 401 as GitHub does. The `agy` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and its terms, `AGY_CLI_DISABLE_AUTO_UPDATE` in a login shell and `agy --help`; then, in a home of its own and with no route out, it starts `agy` in tmux, requires the menu of ways to sign in, chooses Google OAuth, and requires Google's sign-in address and the prompt for the code, and requires that no process of the program is left once tmux has ended. The `muse` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and the terms beside it, `muse --help`, and its screen in tmux, in a home of its own: the question whether to trust the directory, the answer recorded in `trust.json`, the two sign-ins it offers with no credential, and its end, not signed in, at Esc. The `claude` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and Anthropic's notice, the first line of `claude --help`, `claude update`, which the managed settings refuse without fetching a release, and the version after it, and `claude auth status` with no account signed in; it needs no network. The `codex` row checks the pinned version, the program the path finds and its license, `codex login status` with no account signed in and `codex exec --help`, then starts Codex in tmux from a home with no `~/.codex` and requires the sign-in menu, with sign-in by a device code, while Codex is one process, run from `/opt/codex/bin/codex`, with no copy in `~/.codex/packages`, and last that `codex features list` says the background server is off. The `procfd` row requires `/proc/self/fd` to be a directory, as the loops' `tools/flow/scratch.pl` needs to find the scratch a process uses; `tests/run host` runs the tests of the loops' scripts. The `worker-session` row runs the worker loop itself, `tools/flow/worker.sh` from a clone of a bare copy of a git repository of the tree's tests and tools as its `origin`, with Claude Code against the fake server and `gh` on the path a stand-in, [`fakegh.py`](../../../tests/system/agents/fakegh.py), that serves a board of one phase In progress and two of its tasks, #901 and #902, and closes an issue when a commit that closes it reaches the origin's master, as GitHub does. The loop takes #901, and its session, playing [`worker-session.json`](../../../tests/system/agents/worker-session.json), commits on the issue's branch with `Closes #901` and pushes; the loop finds the issue closed, deletes its merged branch and takes #902, whose session commits, pushes, comments and hands the issue back with `board.sh release`. Once the second session has started the row writes the loop's stop file. [`worker_session_verify.py`](../../../tests/system/agents/worker_session_verify.py) judges on the host every recorded request against its step, the worker's prompt for each issue in its session's first request, the loop's log, the board and the calls made to `gh`, the three commits of the origin's master, each session's result and Anthropic's digest of the program. `sh tests/system/agents_mutate.sh` proves the `gh` and `muse` rows against a fault in each recipe, the `claude` row against managed settings that set `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` in place of `DISABLE_UPDATES`, the `codex` row against settings that leave the background server on, the `agy` row against a profile script that sets `AGY_CLI_DISABLE_AUTO_UPDATE` to false, the `claude-print` and `claude-screen` rows against a kernel whose paths do not go on past `/proc/PID/fd/N`, through which Claude Code's Bash tool makes its files, the `worker-session` row against a `worker.sh` that leaves `@ISSUE@` in its session's prompt, the `codex-screen` row against the settings that leave Codex's background server on, which outlives the screen, and, in a run of their own, the `codex-exec` and `codex-screen` rows against settings that set `sandbox_mode` to `workspace-write`, which runs the model's commands in a sandbox that Rach2 cannot make. `sh tests/system/agents_mutate.sh FAULT...` proves the rows of the faults named alone.

`ARCH=x86_64 tests/run agentsaccept` runs the acceptance of the Lenovo, under [Use](#use), in its QEMU mode: on `os-real-gnu-agents.ext2` with 4 GiB of memory, as the test account, with the dummy keys and settings that point every program at the fake API server, whose names the machine's `/etc/hosts` gives. The server plays [`tests/system/accept/agents/AGENT.json`](../../../tests/system/accept/agents) for each program: its `session` while the agent works in its screen, the exchange of the agents suite's rows on the shared fixture, followed by a turn that runs `sleep 600`, and its `after` for the request after the reboot. The steps and their checks are those on the Lenovo, and each program's script must pass as well, every step played and no request it does not have. Each agent cancels a running command with Escape; Codex leaves the command running in a background terminal, which its `/stop` ends. Claude Code reopens with `--continue`, Codex with `resume --last`, Antigravity CLI with `--continue` and Muse Code with `resume --last`, and none asks the model anything to show the conversation again. `sh tests/system/accept/agents_accept_mutate.sh` proves the suite with Claude Code alone against a kernel whose pseudo-terminal master sends no `SIGWINCH` when sshd sets the window's size, after which the machine's tmux never learns that the terminal was resized.

The `muse` row then runs `muse exec --yolo`, and `muse-tmux` runs the same script in the interactive screen, in a fresh home and a clone of the shared fixture: read `notes.txt`, run `check.sh`, edit `greeting.txt` and commit. The server checks each tool result before the next turn. The host checks the returned file, committed tree, author, two commits and clean work tree. It also checks the binary's digest before and after each session, with an empty environment except the test settings. `sh tests/system/muse_session_mutate.sh` requires both modes to reject a commit with the wrong author and to pass before and after that fault.

The test sets `endpoint_transport.base_url`, `endpoint_transport.auth` to `"bearer"` and `endpoint_transport.ca_bundle` in the settings file; the interactive program requires the first two together before sending a key to a custom server. It also sets `tui.prompt_hint_enabled` to false: with it on, the interactive program asks the model to choose a feature tip once a turn has ended and the screen has been idle a few seconds, a request whose time depends on how soon the row ends the session. Headless mode makes six requests. Interactive mode fetches the model catalog twice and probes `/muse-code/config?channel=public`, then makes the same five model requests. The catalog replies use the public Model API's list of models. The config path has no published protocol, so the test answers it with an empty HTTP 404; the session continues without that service. The shared [Responses script](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/muse.json) supplies both modes; the interactive row's script filter adds only these startup exchanges.

Measured on the testing host in a 4096 MiB x86-64 guest, with TCG and two processors, on Muse Code's pinned version above. The digest check caches the binary's file before the session. Free frames are sampled from `/proc/vmstat` once a second; a frame is 4096 bytes. The fall is from the first sample to the smallest. These measurements set no pass criterion.

| Mode | Session (s) | Minimum sampled free frames | Fall from start (KiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `exec` | 43 | 894906 | 117420 |
| `tmux` | 52 | 889516 | 233460 |

The host samples request arrival every 0.1 s. Each interval below starts at the request that selects the tool and ends at the request containing its result, including the HTTPS exchange and tool execution.

| Mode | Read (s) | First check (s) | Edit (s) | Check and commit (s) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `exec` | 4.1 | 7.1 | 4.5 | 6.7 |
| `tmux` | 5.0 | 7.5 | 6.7 | 5.9 |

The `claude-print` and `claude-screen` rows have Claude Code play the exchange of [`claude-session.json`](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/claude-session.json) as the test account, in a fresh home and the fixture's repository, once with `claude -p` and once in its screen in tmux. There the row answers the questions of its first start (the theme, the key in `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, the security notes, trust in the directory and the bypass of its permissions) with the keys a person would press, types the request and ends the session with `/exit`; the script filter adds the screen's own requests, two checks that Anthropic's services answer and the session's title. Asked to, Claude Code reads the fixture, runs a command, edits the file and commits it with git, and the fake server checks each tool result before it answers. [`claude_session_verify.py`](../../../tests/system/agents/claude_session_verify.py) judges the returned file and commit and every recorded request on the host as the Linux proof does, and requires Anthropic's digest of the program before and after the session. The settings are those of the Linux proof, with the fake server as the gateway that `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` names; every host name Claude Code reaches as shipped, listed under [claude](#claude), is the fake server's too, so a request to any of them that the script does not have fails the row, and the machine has no route anywhere else. While a session runs, the row requires the process to run `/opt/claude/bin/claude` with no `LD_` variable in its environment, no `/etc/ld.so.preload`, and no file mapped but the program, the six libraries of glibc it links against and the linker's cache, `/etc/ld.so.cache`.

Measured as for Muse Code, on Claude Code's pinned version, one run of each row: the digest check caches the program's file before the session, and free frames are sampled from `/proc/vmstat` once a second. A session needs about 250 MB of memory. The screen's session includes the row's answers to the questions of the first start: the first question came after 6 s and the prompt after 34 s, the answer was on the screen after 45 s and the session ended at 48 s. With `claude -p` the fixture was edited after 10 s. These measurements set no pass criterion.

| Mode | Session (s) | Free frames at the start | Minimum sampled free frames | Fall from start (KiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `claude -p` | 11 | 967758 | 904660 | 252392 |
| screen | 48 | 948538 | 886744 | 247176 |

The intervals are measured as for Muse Code. In the screen the first turn and the request for the title came together, and the read is counted from the first of the two.

| Mode | Read (s) | Check (s) | Edit (s) | Commit (s) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |

The `agy-print` and `agy-screen` rows have Antigravity CLI play the exchange of [`agy-session.json`](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/agy-session.json) as the test account, in a fresh home and the fixture's repository, once with `agy -p` and once in its screen in tmux. There the row answers the questions of its first start (a color scheme, consent to Google's use of the person's interactions, which the program offers given and the row withholds, and trust in the directory) with the keys a person would press, types the request and ends the session with `/exit`. Asked to, the program reads the fixture, runs a command, edits the file and commits it with git, and the fake server checks each function response before it answers. [`agy_session_verify.py`](../../../tests/system/agents/agy_session_verify.py) judges the returned file and commit and every recorded request on the host as the Linux proof does, and requires Google's digest of the program before and after the session. The settings are those of the Linux proof, with the fake server as the Gemini API that `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` names. The Gemini API's own name, `generativelanguage.googleapis.com`, and the names of the two services the program reaches beside it, listed under [agy](#agy), are the fake server's too: [`agy-services.json`](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/agy-services.json) answers the feature flags' two requests and the usage events with 404 however often they come, so a request to any of these names that the script does not have fails the row, and the machine has no route anywhere else. While a session runs, the row requires the process to run `/opt/agy/bin/agy` with no `LD_` variable in its environment, no `/etc/ld.so.preload`, and no file mapped but the program, glibc's linker and the six libraries it links against, the linker's cache and the shared memory of its SQLite databases, the summaries of its conversations and one for each conversation. `sh tests/system/agy_session_mutate.sh` requires both rows to reject a script that has the program write `answer=afterward`, which every check of a function response still passes, and to pass before and after that fault.

Measured as for Muse Code, on Antigravity CLI's pinned version, in the last of several runs of each row; the others were within 6 MB and 2 s. A session needs about 300 MB of memory with `agy -p` and 245 MB in the screen. The screen's session includes the row's answers to the questions of its first start: the first question came after 6 s and the prompt after 48 s, the answer was on the screen after 56 s and the session ended at 58 s. With `agy -p` the fixture was edited after 8 s. Beside the conversation, the program registered with the feature-flag server and fetched the flags once in each session, and posted usage events 3 times with `agy -p` and 6 times in the screen. These measurements set no pass criterion.

| screen | 58 | 940777 | 879835 | 243768 |

The `codex-exec` and `codex-screen` rows have Codex play the exchange of [`codex.json`](../../../tests/system/fakeapi/codex.json) as the test account, in a fresh home and a clone of the shared fixture, once with `codex exec` and once in its screen in tmux. There the row answers the two questions of the first start, whether to trust the repository and whether to try a newer model than `gpt-5.5`, which it keeps, with the keys a person would press, types the request and ends the session with `/quit`; the script filter adds the screen's own requests, the notice it fetches as it starts and the session's title, which it asks for on a connection of its own, a WebSocket and then a POST. Asked to, Codex reads `notes.txt` and runs `check.sh` over a WebSocket, goes on over HTTPS when the server refuses the next WebSocket with 426, edits `greeting.txt` with `apply_patch`, runs `check.sh` again and commits, and the fake server checks each tool result before it answers. [`codex_session_verify.py`](../../../tests/system/agents/codex_session_verify.py) judges the returned file and commit and every recorded request on the host, and requires before and after the session the digest of `bin/codex` in the package the recipe pins. Codex reaches the fake server through a model provider in `~/.codex/config.toml`, with a dummy key, and its sandbox is off by `/etc/codex/config.toml`; every host name it reaches as shipped, listed under [codex](#codex), is the fake server's too, so a request the script does not have fails the row, and the home's settings turn off its plugins. The row logs in first, as a person does, and gives Codex the address of the session bus the login's profile starts. While a session runs, the row requires the process to run `/opt/codex/bin/codex` with no `LD_` variable in its environment, no `/etc/ld.so.preload`, and no file mapped but the program, the time zone and the shared memory of its SQLite databases in `~/.codex`. Once the session has ended, no process may be left that has in its environment the variable the row gave Codex, or runs a program under `/opt/codex` or the session's directory, where Codex copies itself to start its background server.

Measured as for Muse Code, on Codex's pinned version, one run of each row. A session needs about 140 MB of memory. With `codex exec` the greeting was edited after 9 s and the session ended after 11 s. In the screen the trust question came after 6 s and the prompt after 22 s; the answer was on the screen after 32 s and Codex had ended at 34 s. These measurements set no pass criterion.

| Mode | Session (s) | Free frames at the start | Minimum sampled free frames | Fall from start (KiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `codex exec` | 13 | 967157 | 931264 | 143572 |
| screen | 35 | 951040 | 915525 | 142060 |
